sections.COMMENTS:
The subduction of oceanic crust in the Calabrian Arc began about 80 Ma ago (Faccenna et al., 2001) and currently continues along a rather small sector (~150 km) of the arc between the Isthmus of Catanzaro to the north, and the Strait of Messina to the south. The effect of the NNW-SSE plate convergence upon subduction gradually decreased with the progressive rotation and south-eastward migration of the Calabrian Arc due to continental collision in Sicily (Cifelli et al., 2008).
The southwestern margin of the subduction interface is characterized by a complex structural setting. Near the Alfeo Seamount, its lateral continuity is interrupted by a system of NW-SE high-angle faults, NE-side down (Maesano et al., 2017). This fault system consists of a single major fault south of the Alfeo Seamount and of a more complex en-echelon fault array to the northwest. This fault system cuts the entire Ionian crust at least down to the Moho, with increasing displacement from SE to NW and is interpreted as the Subduction Edge Propagator (STEP, sensu Govers and Wortel, 2005) of the Calabrian subduction zone tentatively identified by Polonia et al. (2011).
To the northwest, a NNW-trending oblique dextral  fault set known as the Tindari Fault System (or â€œTindari-Letojanni Lineâ€�) runs from the Gulf of Patti along the northern shoulder of the Mt. Etna volcano across  the Peloritani Mts. (Cultrera et al., 2017). It could represent the upper plate deformation due to the presence of the STEP fault system at the southwestern edge of the Calabrian subduction system. This fault also cuts towards southeast into the Ionian Sea (Nicolich et al., 2000). It is thought to accommodate the differential motion between the collisional Sicilian orogen and the retreating Calabrian slab with transtensional to strike slip movements.
Historical and instrumental catalogues (ISIDe Working Group, 2007; Guidoboni et al., 2019; Rovida et al., 2021) show a sparse intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.5) seismicity all over this region, including the damaging earthquakes that hit the northern sector of the source on 28 March 1780 (Mw 5.5) Sicilia Nord-orientale, and on 10 March 1786 (Mw 6.1) Golfo di Patti.
Given its position at the boundary between extension in the Messina Straits (to the northeast) and compression (to the southwest), we believe that this structure holds a key seismogenic potential.
